input:
The benchmark material is also the subject of a disagreement over selectivity that the published values, taken at face value, do not resolve. Two groups have reported values for the same material class that differ substantially, and it would be misleading to average them or to treat the spread as ordinary experimental noise, because the groups did not obtain their numbers in the same way. In one case, the reported selectivity was predicted from measurements on the separate pure components, with IAST used to estimate how the components would behave together in the adsorbed phase; the prediction therefore inherits the assumptions built into that treatment, including the treatment of mixing in the adsorbed phase itself. In the other case, selectivity was measured with mixtures directly, so that competition between the components for adsorption sites was part of the observation rather than an assumption added during the analysis. Direct mixture measurement is closer to the conditions of an actual separation, which counts in its favour, but it is also exposed to drift in feed composition and to doubt about whether equilibrium had genuinely been reached when the measurement was taken. Weighing these considerations, the mixture-based values deserve a limited preference, since the effect that decides the separation is present in the measurement. The preference is, however, conditional in an important respect: it rests on the mixture measurements having been made at feed compositions close to the intended separation and on equilibrium having been demonstrated, and where either of those conditions is absent the preference loses its basis.

For a reader, the practical consequence is that the test conditions have to be reported beside each value, since a figure from one route cannot be placed directly against a figure from the other without them.
target:
Selectivity values for the benchmark material differ substantially between the two groups, and the published values do not resolve the disagreement at face value. Averaging the values would mislead: the groups did not obtain their numbers in the same way, and the spread is not ordinary experimental noise. One group predicted selectivity from measurements on the separate pure components, using IAST to estimate how the components behave together in the adsorbed phase. A prediction of that kind inherits the assumptions of the treatment, including the treatment of mixing in the adsorbed phase. The other group measured selectivity with mixtures directly. Competition between the components for adsorption sites was part of the observation, not an assumption added during the analysis. Direct mixture measurement stands closer to the conditions of an actual separation. Mixture measurement carries its own weaknesses: feed composition can drift during a run, and equilibrium at the point of measurement can be in doubt. The mixture-based values carry a limited preference, because the effect that decides the separation is present in the measurement itself. The preference rests on two conditions. Feed compositions in the mixture measurements must lie close to the intended separation, and equilibrium must be demonstrated. Where either condition is absent, the preference loses its basis, and the two sets of values stand unresolved.

Test conditions therefore belong beside each reported value. A selectivity figure without its route of measurement, its feed basis and its equilibrium evidence cannot be placed against a figure obtained by the other route. The disagreement is a disagreement about values obtained under different conditions. The disagreement is not a contradiction between two measurements of the same state.
